confirmed_observations: HIA checksum loop has a separate per-byte index/buffer-length bounds branch plus checked-add overflow branch; both Rust variants retain checked-add overflow but no corresponding per-byte bounds branch.
All three implementations have a 16-byte vector fill loop; Rust variants additionally have a four-byte vector epilogue.
At the frozen 4093-byte input, HIA has 13 scalar tail stores; the Rust variants use three four-byte vector tail stores then one scalar store.
All three checksum loops remain scalar and use unsigned-add overflow checking.

HIA calls calloc for this function; both Rust variants retain bulk memset(size-1) plus a last-byte zero store before the fill. Constructor-only zero-elision diagnosis therefore does not establish a unique full_lifecycle zeroing cost.
inference: HIA extracts buffer length and success from an aggregate allocation-result PHI and retains size and length as distinct SSA values. This is consistent with the optimizer failing to prove their equality; it is not a formally established sole cause.
not_established: No causal percentage of the noisy 1.333/1.309 ratios is attributed to a specific instruction.
No claim that HIA lacks vectorization or Rust drops integer safety checks.
Allocator/library differences, LLVM 20.1.2 versus 20.1.8, and shared-host noise have not been isolated.
No new compiler optimization, benchmark rerun, or passing P5 result.
